title: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown

fields.label: Label
fields.value: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Growth curves in other animals”. Scope: animals generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The phase sequence is measurable, and open databases permit broad tests for selected vertebrates. Existing standardized trajectories do not cover animals generally, so the universal generalization cannot be fully resolved without major compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit size-at-age and growth-velocity curves from birth or hatching to adulthood across animal taxa, then test for the shared sequence of slow onset, early velocity maximum and terminal slowdown. Taxa with maximal growth late or persistent nonzero adult growth would refute universality.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Comparable raw longitudinal growth curves are scattered.

Birth, hatching and growth cessation differ fundamentally across taxa.

The universal wording is vulnerable to poorly sampled exceptions.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.7
data existence: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A common sequence of a slow start, an early peak, and a slowdown is visible in compiled growth trajectories for many vertebrates, and longevity databases classify the life-span contrast the claim draws. The universal quantifier over all animals is not matched by the taxonomic coverage, and the most common fisheries growth model assumes away the early lag. The phases can be recovered for a biased but substantial subset if raw series are used instead of those fits.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From age-length or age-weight series, locate the age of maximum growth velocity and the later decline toward cessation, in both long-lived and short-lived species. An early maximum followed by slowdown would support the shared sequence; a maximum at the start of growth, or no slowdown, in a large clade would limit the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Invertebrates are much less completely measured than mammals and commercial fishes.

Von Bertalanffy fits force the maximum growth rate to the origin and can hide an early slow start.
